title: Multi-agent discovery of practical quantum LDPC codes
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can encode multiple logical qubits using sparse parity checks, yet searching for useful finite-length instances remains a challenging design problem because code performance must be optimized while satisfying practical constraints. Motivated by recent advances in artificial-intelligence agents for scientific discovery, we develop a multi-agent framework for discovering practical qLDPC codes. The framework combines specialist proposal and review, persistent scientific memory, long-horizon evolution of executable programs, and deterministic construction and evaluation within a closed-loop search. These programs instantiate coset-orbit balanced-product codes, providing a search space that includes bicycle and lifted-product constructions as well as non-normal subgroup actions. To incorporate practical constraints, we restrict the search to binary CSS codes with block length $n\leq400$ and overall weight $w\leq10$. Within this regime, the framework discovers codes with leading or competitive rate--distance performance in every weight class considered, with representative instances including $[[288,16,18]]$ at $w=7$, $[[288,18,18]]$ at $w=9$, and $[[234,28,18]]$ at $w=10$. The search also uncovers structurally distinct, high-performing constructions, including a $[[336,12,\leq24]]$ candidate and a $[[368,18,16]]$ code, both of which are genuine balanced-product constructions with non-normal subgroup actions. When evaluated under code-capacity depolarizing noise using a common BP-OSD decoding protocol, the discovered codes also exhibit low logical failure rates. Together, these results provide hardware-relevant finite-length candidates for further experimental evaluation and show how structured agentic search can contribute to scientific discovery.
summary: This paper introduces a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework designed to overcome the difficult search problem associated with finding practical Quantum LDPC codes. By combining specialist proposal, memory retention, and iterative program execution, the agents efficiently discover high-performing code candidates. These results provide concrete, hardware-relevant quantum error correction resources for future experimental implementation.
main_problem: The core challenge is designing practical, finite-length Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes that achieve optimal performance while satisfying strict hardware constraints.
main_result: The developed multi-agent framework successfully discovers several high-performing, structurally distinct qLDPC code candidates with competitive rate-distance trade-offs for various weight classes.
method: A novel multi-agent AI framework is employed in a closed loop to search the space of coset-orbit balanced-product codes, optimizing performance metrics against practical constraints like block length and overall weight.
model_or_system: The work focuses on quantum error correction using qLDPC codes. These codes encode logical qubits by distributing information across physical qubits via sparse parity checks, which are constructed using specific algebraic structures derived from finite groups.
key_observables: Code parameters $[[n, k, d]]$ (block length, encoded qubits, distance), the rate ($k/n$), and a composite performance metric $Q = k d^2 / n$.
important_parameters: Constraints include binary CSS codes with block length $n \le 400$ and overall weight $w \le 10$. Performance is evaluated under code-capacity depolarizing noise.
main_assumptions: The search relies on the assumption that structured agentic AI can efficiently explore complex combinatorial spaces, and performance evaluation uses established decoding protocols (BP-OSD) and distance estimation techniques (QDistEvol).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the multi-agent discovery framework loop. Figure 2 organizes comparative results for discovered codes across different overall-weight classes ($w$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the multi-agent search methodology (combining proposal/review loops), presents the construction space (coset-orbit balanced-product codes), reports key findings with specific code examples and performance metrics, and concludes by validating the approach's utility for hardware design.
why_interesting: The application of advanced AI techniques to systematically discover optimal quantum error correction codes is highly relevant. It provides a blueprint for using computational intelligence to solve fundamental theoretical limits in quantum computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The multi-agent discovery framework. A scientific-reasoning loop (top) uses researcher proposals, curator synthesis and persistent memory to generate exploration and validation tasks. A program-evolution loop (bottom) mutates executable qLDPC-family generators within a MAP-Elites archive and scores candidates using a fixed evaluator. Evaluated candidates update both the archive and the evidence available to the scientific loop. L1–L4 denote mutations of local terms, protographs, subgroups and host groups, respectively.

Figure 2: Finite-length performance under overall-weight constraints. Panels (a)–(e) compare the parameter score 𝑄= 𝑘𝑑2/𝑛against block length 𝑛at fixed overall weights 𝑤= 6–10. Purple circles are codes discovered in this work and gray squares are literature codes; filled markers denote exact distances and open markers denote QDistEvol distance upper bounds, for which the plotted 𝑄is an upper endpoint. Selected discoveries from Table I are labeled with their [[𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑]] parameters, including the exact-distance leaders [[288, 16, 18]], [[288, 18, 18]] and [[234, 28, 18]] at 𝑤= 7, 9 and 10.

Figure 3: Code-capacity performance under depolarizing noise. (a) Block error rate 𝑝block and (b) per- logical error rate 𝜖𝐿versus the physical error rate 𝑝for four discovered codes at 𝑤= 6 and 7 (solid purple: [[288, 16, 18]], [[336, 12, 20]], [[384, 16, ≤24]] and [[400, 16, ≤22]]) and two weight-six bivariate-bicycle benchmarks (dashed gray: [[288, 12, 18]] and [[360, 12, ≤24]]), all decoded with the same minimum-sum BP–OSD protocol. The dashed line in (a) marks 𝑝block = 𝑝, whose crossing defines the pseudo-threshold. Error bars are exact 95% confidence intervals; points with no observed failures are plotted as open markers at their upper confidence limits.
